June marks Immigrant Heritage Month.

At Jordan Community School in Rogers Park, more than 60% of the 484 students are English language learners. Families come from dozens of countries and speak more than 30 languages.

For many families, everything about this country is brand new, including the worry of whether a school will truly accept them for who they are. Belonging isn't just a buzzword; it's an action, visible in the quiet, everyday choices a school makes behind the scenes.

When a student shared that her family assumed the school would not decorate for Ramadan, Principal Chris Graves did not just say yes. He asked the students to teach him how.

"I wouldn't know how to decorate, so I need you to teach me,” Principal Graves said.

This inclusive approach became an annual tradition, with the holiday calendar now mapped out together.

The commitment to inclusion extends throughout the building. When Principal Graves noticed Muslim families were receiving limited meal options at school events, he ensured halal options were available at every gathering so no family would ever have to eat separately from the rest. As more Swahili-speaking students enrolled, a Swahili language program followed. And as the student body grew more diverse, a former storage room was transformed into a library stocked so that every student can find characters who look like them.

Heritage is not only honored in celebration. It is honored when a leader treats a family's culture as something to build around, not work around.

We honor school leaders like Principal Graves, whose curiosity and inclusivity inspire a sense of true belonging in their communities.

This week, we’re proud to spotlight Nancy Quintana, principal at Finkl Elementary School and a member of our 2025–26 Malott Educator Fellowship cohort.

Principal Quintana leads Finkl with the kind of deep care that makes students, families, and staff feel seen, known, and supported. This year, she has translated that care into action by strengthening Tier 1 attendance structures, which include building a positive school culture, using universal data tracking, and proactively preventing chronic absenteeism.

According to ISBE, IAR proficiency at Finkl increased from 32.7% in 2021 to 44.5% in 2025, while chronic absenteeism decreased roughly seven percentage points from 2024 to 2025. Finkl’s K–2 cluster classroom was also recognized as a district Model of Excellence, drawing educators from across Chicago Public Schools to learn from the school’s practices and approach.

Beyond the classroom, scholars with disabilities are thriving through expanded opportunities to lead, compete, and create. This year, students revived a school coffee shop, participated in the Special Olympics, joined Robotics4All, and created artwork on permanent display at the district’s Office for Students with Disabilities.

Principal Quintana’s leadership extends beyond her school community as she also serves as CPAA Auxiliary 4 President for Networks 7 and 8. Through every initiative, she is helping build a school where every system reflects a simple but powerful belief: every student belongs.

Over the past few weeks, our CEO Heather Anichini has walked through several major drivers shaping CPS school budgets in FY27.

In May, CPS announced a $732M deficit for FY27, up from the $520M projected in the FY26 Budget Book.

School-level budgets absorb nearly $100M of that gap. How CPS closes the rest is still an open question.

Today's budget update: The Opportunity Index (OI)

The OI is CPS's equity-based formula for directing resources to schools with greater student and community needs. Each school receives a score based on 11 metrics tied to student demographics, community characteristics, and historical funding levels.

In FY26, scores ranged from 11 to 47. Higher scores indicate greater relative need and generally lead to more resources.
Higher need = more teaching positions.

OI scores are relative and shift year to year. For schools near a threshold, even a small change can trigger significant budget impact.

Principals have until June 9 to appeal allocations, work with their Local School Councils, and finalize budgets. The district has until August 29 to pass a budget for FY27.

Follow Heather on LinkedIn for more insight on the OI, enrollment shifts, revised staffing ratios, and more.

➡️Chronic absenteeism declined from 27.4% in 2024 to 24.3% in 2025. 

By leading with transparency about her own growth as a leader, principal Militello has helped foster a culture where staff feel empowered to contribute, collaborate, and lead alongside administration. Last weekend, CPS principals Lourdes Jimenez and Javier Arriola-Lopez led Pause and Reflect: Sustaining the Spark on Your Dual Language Roadmap — a Learning Lab designed to help school leaders audit their Dual Language programs, identify strengths and areas of improvement, and walk away with a clear, actionable plan before summer break.

👏 "I truly enjoyed the presentation by Mr. Arriola and Ms. Jimenez,” said Jose Rodriguez, Assistant Principal of Rachel Carson Elementary. “They provided us with ample time to plan and reflect on our school's mission and vision and how it connects with our Dual Language goals. 👏 "This is an excellent opportunity for other leaders to attend. It is a space where you can reflect and think about what the next steps will be to enhance the dual language program or TBE program,” said Cesar Lopez, teacher leader at North Grand High School. “The best part is that all school leaders benefit from this workshop regardless of their experience and knowledge."

The timing is intentional. By reflecting now, leaders have the tools to mobilize their teams and resources while staff are still in the building — paving the foundation for schools to hit the ground running in the fall.

This is what peer-led learning looks like in practice: school leaders who are doing the work, opening the door for others to strengthen theirs.

Denise Little led Hefferan Elementary for 13 years. Before that, she was a classroom teacher, worked in computer science, and one of the first principals in her network to build a data-driven reading system from the ground up. By the time she retired as a CPS Network Chief, she'd spent decades developing teachers, developing principals, and refusing to accept less than excellence for the children she served.

She believes this job requires backbone.

"I think what they get wrong is that you have to compromise your beliefs. You have to be “nice.” What you actually have to have is backbone. You have to be a visionary. You have to be relational. And most of all, you have to be fair."

For Denise, fairness meant walking across a bridge. When she noticed a school across the expressway was outperforming hers – with the same demographics, she didn't just accept it. She went and asked what they were doing differently. The answer was data. She learned it, brought it back, and eventually scaled it to 25 schools across her network.

"I wanted the best for my students, too."

Denise retired, but the techniques she learned and taught are still running through schools across Chicago. The principals she developed are still leading. The standard she set is excellence as a starting point, not a finish line. That is still the expectation.

That's not just leadership. That's legacy.

This Women's History Month, we honor the leaders who helped build Chicago's educational foundation – one relationship, one system, one principal at a time.

Annette Gurley led Michele Clark Academy for 22 years. Before that, she served as a substitute teacher, classroom teacher, facilitator, and assistant principal. By the time she retired in 2016 as CPS Chief Officer of Teaching and Learning, she'd spent 32 years investing in people.

She believes this job is NOT transactional.

"If you're working in a school in an underserved community and the children are two or three years behind, and you check all those boxes, and they get a year's gain, they're still two or three years behind. So you have to put forth that extra effort."
 
For Annette, that extra effort meant getting out of the office and into classrooms. It meant understanding every staff member's strengths and needs. It meant creating systems that would last long after she left.

"You have to make it safe for them to make mistakes. Because if they think they're going to be penalized for it, they will hide it. And when you hide what you don't know as a teacher, as a student, nobody gains."

Annette retired a decade ago, but the systems she built alongside other CPS leaders are still running. The principals she mentored are still leading. That's not transactional leadership. That's legacy.

"People saw something in me that I didn't see in myself."

Stephen McClain, Ed.D. didn't plan to become a principal. He actually thought he'd be a career-long teacher. But mentors poured into him, including Mr. McComb, the only Black male teacher he ever had—and that changed everything.

As a recent CPS principal, Stephan has always led with purpose. Now, as a Malott Educator Fellowship Coach for The Fund, he's pouring into five principals across four networks with the same intentionality. Over the next year, he's focused on decreasing chronic absence, strengthening leadership effectiveness, and coaching leaders to embody three values: maintaining their joy, increasing students' sense of belonging, and empowering principals to live into their purpose.

"For most Black leaders I know, their why is the Black child in front of them, the Black teacher beside them, the Black family in their school. Let that ground you as well as joy. Because if you don't have joy, you won't last in this work."

This Black History Month, we're celebrating the educators who stay in the fight, and the mentors who make it possible.

Our annual Program Summary report is here, and it tells a story we're proud to share.

This year, The Fund is supporting principals and assistant principals from almost half (298) of the district schools. These leaders are driving real results: growing 5Essentials Effective Leaders scores, reducing chronic absenteeism, and building the sustainable systems that help students thrive.

What makes this work powerful is our intent to listen. When principals tell us what they need, we evolve. That commitment shows up in every program — from the Malott Educator Fellowship that supports Priority School leaders, to Leadership Bridge that helps build a diverse principal pipeline, to our Network Acceleration Strategy that equips principal supervisors with the tools to strengthen leadership across entire networks.

The report features four incredible school leaders and two principal supervisors whose stories demonstrate what's possible when we invest in principals. We're grateful for their commitment and excited to share their impact.

Research is clear: Principals have an outsized impact on student learning. In Chicago, where school leaders have more autonomy than their peers nationwide, that impact is even more pronounced.

Principal LaKenya Sharpe of The Collins Academy High School is transforming school culture and student engagement with her equity-driven leadership.

When she arrived, attendance and motivation were low. By listening to students and staff, she uncovered barriers like a lack of connection to the school, responsibilities outside the classroom, and a lack of programming to meet student interests. She implemented innovative strategies:

▪️Warrior Points incentive system that rewards attendance, behavior, and academics
▪️Partnerships with neighboring elementary schools, coordinating drop-off windows for students who have to take younger siblings to school
▪️Career pathways, including an after-school nail technician program in partnership with a local Black-owned salon

The impact was clear:
▪️40% of students reached top-tier Warrior Points status
▪️Schoolwide attendance rose by 4 percentage points
▪️Disciplinary incidents declined by 80%
▪️Student participation and demand for programs increased, shifting school culture toward engagement and celebration

As Principal Sharpe explains: “When kids feel seen and celebrated, they show up for themselves and for each other.”

Apply this learning: Leaders can integrate student voice into culture-building, design incentives tied to attendance and behavior, and partner creatively to remove barriers to engagement.

Read more about Principal Sharpe and other Chicago Growth Leaders on our blog: https://thefundchicago.org/case-study-growing-a-positive-supportive-culture-at-collins-high-school/

Principal Claudia Ortiz leads Tarkington Elementary School with a commitment to equity, multiculturalism, and strong instruction.

When students returned to in-person learning after school closures during the pandemic, Claudia used data to identify student and staff needs, focusing on English learners and disabled students who were struggling academically and emotionally. She and her team prioritized:

▪️Instructional Coherence: Implementing the Skyline English language arts curriculum (grades 3-8) and aligned Spanish-language materials for K-2 dual-language classrooms, ensuring all students receive high-quality instruction

▪️Distributed Teacher Leadership: Expanding the instructional leadership team and teacher-led professional development, including peer observations and weekly feedback cycles

▪️Targeted Academic & Social-Emotional Learning Support: Strengthening multi-tiered system of supports and the Power of Two initiative for students performing just below grade-level, alongside celebrations, counseling partnerships, and a phone-free policy

The results were measurable and meaningful:

▪️ Tarkington moved from Targeted Support in 2021 to Commendable status in 2024 on the Illinois Report Card

▪️ Behavioral incidents declined

▪️ Student engagement increased

Apply This Learning: Leaders can build curriculum coherence, foster teacher leadership and peer feedback, and ensure equity with targeted academic and social-emotional supports.

Apply This Learning: Leaders can create structured opportunities for student voice, foster peer collaboration among staff, and build consistent family engagement routines.

Principal Venus DeLoach stepped into leadership at Carver Primary School with a vision: Families must be true partners in learning.

When she became principal in 2021, student attendance was at 78% and parent participation was just 24%. Rather than make assumptions, Venus gathered data, interviewed families, and created space for honest dialogue. What she heard reshaped her approach: Parents wanted respect, transparency, and a real voice in their children’s education.

Venus responded by launching Carver’s Very Important Parent (VIP) initiative, reframing report card pickup as Parent Appreciation Day, and tying celebrations to attendance goals. The results were powerful:

▪️Parent participation in report card pickup jumped from 24% to nearly 70%.
▪️Kindergarten attendance rose from the lowest in the school to 94.7%.
▪️Trust between families and staff grew stronger than ever.

“I can’t do this work without them,” Venus explains. “When parents know they’re valued, everything changes.”

Apply This Learning: Leaders can listen to families, connect attendance and celebrations, and create transparent communication to build trust and engagement.

Each year, from September 15 to October 15, we celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month. The dates are significant—September 15 marks the independence anniversaries of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua, followed by Mexico on September 16 and Chile on September 18. This month is a time to honor the rich histories, cultures, and lasting contributions of Hispanic and Latino/a/x communities.

Yet this year, our celebrations are tempered with the realities many face. Families across Chicago and the state continue to navigate heightened concerns around safety and immigration enforcement, which impact the well-being of students and families.

Despite these challenges, the spirit of unity perseveres. School leaders, families, and community leaders continue to stand together, ensuring schools remain sanctuaries of learning and safety.

To further support families, Chicago Public Schools has shared guidance on how to stay safe while traveling to and from school and in the greater community. This resource includes additional information for immigrant families and upcoming Know Your Rights workshops. You can access the full resource here: https://www.cps.edu/globalassets/cps-pages/services-and-supports/new-administration-guidance/resource-packet-for-federal-deployment-english.pdf

In addition, the Latino Policy Forum offers in-person and online workshops in English and Spanish for parents, community members, and potential school partners. These workshops cover Early Childhood Development, K–12 Education, and Higher Education, providing tools and resources to help families navigate the educational landscape. You can access the resource here: https://latinopolicyforum.org/webinars-and-workshops/

Wendell Smith, a school serving low-income and high-needs students, will have five fewer teaching positions next year. As a result, Principal Turan Crockett says every classroom will be overcrowded, making it more difficult to meet student needs and maintain a strong learning environment.

Principal Crockett shared that they’ve scaled back before- and after-school programs and reassigned staff roles to free up minimal funding. Despite being resourceful and creative with past budgets, this year is different—the cuts are deeper, and the consequences more severe.

If CPS continues to face annual deficits and prioritize short-term solutions over sustainable funding, Crockett fears we’ll see school closures and consolidations, especially in communities already facing the greatest barriers to student success.

His message is clear: without real investment and long-term planning, CPS cannot meet the needs of its most vulnerable students. Schools like Wendell Smith are being pushed to the edge, and it's the students who will suffer most.

Juneteenth, originally called Jubilee Day, marks the date June 19, 1865, when the last enslaved people in Galveston, Texas, were finally informed of their freedom. This occurred more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation had been issued. The delay reminds us that freedom delayed is freedom denied, and that access to truth and education is essential to justice.

At the heart of Juneteenth’s modern recognition is Opal Lee, a retired teacher and lifelong activist who believed the story of Black freedom should be known and honored across the country. At 89 years old, she walked from Fort Worth, Texas, to Washington, D.C., to raise awareness and build support. Her efforts helped make Juneteenth a federal holiday in 2021.

Juneteenth is not just about history. It is about how we teach it, remember it, and grow from it. It reminds us that:

▪️ Education has the power to liberate and heal
▪️ We must teach the full story of American history, including its injustices and its progress
▪️ Representation, truth-telling, and inclusion are essential in the classroom

While CPS schools plan for 2025–26, Herzl School of Excellence reminds us what great leadership looks like.

Principal Tamara Davis and team are elevating student voices through monthly SEL themes like “Use Your Voice” — with all students contributing ideas to shape their school.

Principals and Local School Councils are working on their 2025-26 budgets right now, making important decisions about how they support their students. Between budgeting and district leadership transitions, it’s crucial to remember the essential work that schools are doing for students every day.

A perfect example is Principal Tamara Davis and her team at Herzl School of Excellence. They are leading the way in social and emotional learning (SEL) with a thoughtful, school-wide approach that centers student voice and leadership.

Each month, they focus on an SEL theme aligned to the CASEL framework, such as “Be an Upstander,” “Exhibit Patience,” “Embrace a Growth Mindset,” and “Value and Accept Diversity.” The Herzl team promotes these themes throughout the building and supports school-wide activities that bring the learning to life for students in pre-kindergarten through 8th grade.

In April, the SEL theme was "Use Your Voice." On April 25, every student at Herzl had the opportunity to share what they love about their school community and what improvements they’d like to see. Feedback from this school-wide listening activity will be reviewed by the school’s Culture and Climate Team, SEL Team, and Instructional Leadership Team to inform improvements for the 2025-26 school year.

A core value at Herzl is “We Are Leaders.” The school’s belief in collective efficacy and distributed leadership is evident in how both staff and students are empowered to contribute their ideas and strengths. From monthly surveys and check-ins to SEL events and classroom discussions, Principal Davis and the Herzl team ensure that everyone has a voice in shaping the school community.

We’re proud to highlight Herzl’s strong commitment to student voice, equity, and leadership in action.

In September, The Fund launched its 2024-25 cohort of the Local School Council (LSC) Working Group. The group consisted of representatives from 22 schools and 18 networks, with one goal: designing a tool that helps LSCs assess their effectiveness and identify areas for growth.

Together, we explored what strong governance looks like, how LSCs can amplify community voice, and where they need more support. Some key insights:
 ▪️ LSC members feel most impactful when making important school-level decisions, like principal evaluation and selection, addressing student concerns, and helping develop solutions based on school data.

 ▪️ LSCs want more accessible, practical tools, like opportunities to hear peer stories, role-play scenarios, and access to video-based resources.

Congratulations to Chicago Public Schools Chief Education Officer Bogdana Chkoumbova, who announced her plans to leave CPS earlier today. Chief Chkoumbova’s career spanned from special education teacher at Chopin Elementary, to founding principal at Disney II Magnet School, to Chief of Network 10, to the Chief Schools Officer, and culminated with the role of Chief Education Officer. She served in that role for three critical years, leading school communities through COVID-19 recovery and guiding the district through the most recent contract negotiations with the Chicago Teachers Union (CTU).  

Our CEO, Heather Y. Anichini, reflected, “In every role, Chief Chkoumbova remained unwavering in her commitment to the students of Chicago and the transformative power of public education.”  

We have certainly learned a lot from Chief Chkoumbova over the years. The Fund first profiled her successful budgeting practices as a principal in 2015. Her Disney II team joined our inaugural School Design Program cohort, and she was selected as a Chicago Principal Fellow.

As she moved into new district roles, she remained focused on supporting principal leadership citywide. As a Network Chief, Chief Schools Officer, and Chief Education Officer, she worked to understand the needs of principals, align resources to meet those needs, and ensure that principal decision-making was protected. 

Our Director of Education Supports, Mariel Laureano, another former founding principal in CPS, noted that “Chief Choumbova served with me in the first cohort of the Independent Schools Principals program in 2015-16. As her career advanced, I continued to see how she truly championed the importance of school leadership and the incredible results school leaders can achieve with the right support and autonomy. She has been an inspiration and a true leader in the district, and it has been an honor to work with her over the years.”  

Chief Chkoumbova’s focus on student and school data, quality instruction, and school leadership leaves a lasting legacy for CPS students and educators.

We are grateful for her leadership and wish her well in her next chapter.

At SXSW EDU, the Surge Institute's Black Principals Network led a powerful discussion on sustaining the Black principal pipeline. The panel, featuring TaraShaun Gipson, Folasade Adekunle, Kazmir Davis, and David McGuire, explored the critical supports principals need to thrive, focusing on community, restoration, professional growth, and sustainability in school leadership.

▪️ Principals need intentional support structures, from professional networks to executive coaching, to help them navigate the complexities of their roles and prevent burnout.

▪️ Leadership sustainability isn't just about individual resilience—it's about building systems that position principals for success and ensure schools remain strong over time.

▪️ Strong leadership development includes ongoing coaching—not just for new principals but throughout their careers—to move from daily problem-solving to long-term planning.

This conversation reinforced the importance of leadership networks like the Surge Institute's Black Principals Network and The Leadership Collaborative, which provide professional learning and a space for connection, reflection, and shared strategies.

Daniel Perry, a dedicated educator with nearly 20 years of experience in Chicago Public Schools, has played a pivotal role in shaping student success. He has served as a teacher, assistant principal, principal, deputy chief of schools, and chief of schools. Notably, as principal at Wacker Elementary, he led the school from probationary to non-probationary status within just two years, improving student performance by 3% in reading and 7% in mathematics. As Deputy Chief of Network 13, Daniel applied restorative practices that increased student performance in English Language Arts by 2% and reduced school suspensions by 50%.

Currently, Daniel serves as the facilitator of The Fund’s Black Affinity Group, a role that has allowed him to engage in dynamic discussions and collaborate on strategies for leadership development. The group’s first session focused on leadership self-reflection, where emerging school leaders identified their strengths and areas for growth. The second session emphasized the importance of self-care for school leaders, recognizing that their well-being directly impacts their ability to serve students effectively.

"I've been particularly energized by the insightful discussions, collaboration, and impactful strategies that have emerged. The research tells us that Black leaders are more adversely affected healthwise due to the challenges of leadership. It is critical that school leaders are aware and have strategies to adapt to take care of themselves," said Daniel.

Looking ahead, the group will dive into key topics like culturally responsive curriculum, principal readiness, and school budgeting. Each leader will also create a personalized development plan outlining the critical skills and experiences needed to reach the next level of leadership.

This Black History Month, we celebrate the dedication and leadership of those who have significantly contributed to educational equity in our communities.

At Avalon Park Fine and Performing Arts School, Principal Takeshi James and her team are leading a transformative shift in how students learn. Avalon Park is one of four Chicago magnet schools that are sharing a $15 million federal grant, and they are using those funds to implement a personalized learning model. As reported by the Chicago Tribune, this model allows students to co-design their own learning paths with teachers based on their individual strengths, needs, and interests. The full implementation of personalized learning will begin in the 2025-26 school year and continue through 2028-29.

In addition to this shift, Avalon Park has become a hub of interactive learning. Walking up to the school's second floor, students encounter what is now called "Ms. Leachman’s Diner" and "Ms. Strahan’s Food Court". These imaginary restaurants, set up with gingham-clothed tables and rearranged booths, provide students with a hands-on approach to learning math concepts like percentages and ratios. This creative, real-world application is just one of the many ways the school is making education more relevant and interactive for students.

This type of approach is not new to Avalon Park. In 2022, Principal James and her team participated in The Fund's Summer Design Program to address significant academic gaps for students caused by the pandemic. They implemented a summer initiative focused on interactive math experiences with real-world applications, beginning with math fluency drills to strengthen basic skills and culminating in students designing math board games. This hands-on approach helped set the stage for the ongoing shift to personalized learning. Over time, the lessons from that summer initiative have continued to evolve and influence the school's personalized learning model, creating a more tailored and student-centered approach to education at Avalon Park.

This Black History Month, we celebrate the power of innovative initiatives like this one, which empower Black and brown students to discover their strengths and reach their full potential. By creating personalized, engaging learning experiences, we ensure that every student can thrive in a system that is increasingly responsive to their unique needs.

Statement on the December 20th Special Meeting of the Chicago Board of Education by The Chicago Public Education Fund:

"At The Fund, we help educators navigate complex school-based challenges, including leadership transitions. Replacing a principal requires time, thoughtful planning, and open communication with the affected communities. We invest in these efforts because poorly managed leadership changes can disrupt student learning. The adverse effects persist for more than two years.

Leadership transitions at the top of a school district affect every student, school, and community in the system. Over the past several months, hundreds of school leaders have voiced concerns about a potential leadership change in Chicago Public Schools (CPS). If such a transition occurs, CPS’s 320,000 students deserve a process that is strategic, transparent, and well-communicated. This cannot be achieved through board meetings called on short notice with limited public input.

In the last 25 years, The Fund has supported the CPS community through 10 CEO transitions. We have seen how challenging it becomes for school leaders to maintain focus when district-level changes create instability and distraction. Given the potential harm that a rushed decision could cause to principals, students, and school communities, we urge the Chicago Board of Education to delay any consideration of CPS CEO Pedro Martinez’s employment status. They are responsible for ensuring a transparent process grounded in meaningful community engagement and stakeholder input. Students’ educational success depends on their leadership in this critical moment."

In August, Erin Walker began her second year as principal of Infinity Math, Science, and Technology High School, an early-college STEM school in Chicago's Little Village. Over the summer, she engaged with the school community to establish a shared vision, focusing on rewriting the school's mission and vision statements. Having previously served as assistant principal, Erin views this initiative as a crucial step in her transition to school leadership.

Her shift from the classroom to administration was initially unexpected. After spending 16 years as a teacher, she had not envisioned becoming a principal. However, her journey took a new direction when she pursued the assistant principal position at Infinity, where she discovered fulfillment in both supporting students and teachers. Every day, Erin brings her memories of being a classroom teacher with her through Infinity's front doors. "If you're working with teachers, you can't forget what it's like to be a teacher," she stresses. 

As principal, Erin aims to empower her staff while keeping student needs at the forefront. During Principal Appreciation Month, her journey highlights the courage and commitment of leaders who embrace new roles, ultimately transforming the experiences of their students and communities.

Principal Vincent Izuegbu is in his fourth year as principal of Ida B. Wells Preparatory Elementary Academy, an IB World School committed to giving Bronzeville students a global perspective. Each year, he leads students on international trips, visiting a country in Europe and one in Africa. In 2025, the destinations are Spain and South Africa, reinforcing the school’s mission to connect students with their roots and broaden their horizons. With 91.1% of the student body identifying as Black, these trips are designed to help students explore their heritage and foster resilience, reminding them of their ancestral journey. In October, during Principal Appreciation Month, his image appears on buses, highlighting his dedication to education and the vital role of school leaders.

Vincent’s leadership is shaped by his experiences and his mother’s influence as an educator. He emphasizes the importance of integrity and fairness in building trust within the school community. Under his guidance, Wells Prep has formed partnerships that pave the way for students to earn college credit, ensuring a pipeline from pre-K to higher education. 

With accolades such as being one of Chicago’s two Apple Distinguished Schools, Vincent is focused on fostering global citizenship among students, aiming to empower them to tackle real-world challenges like environmental sustainability and social issues, ultimately shaping compassionate, informed leaders for the future.

Read more about Principal Vincent Izuegbu on our blog: https://thefundchicago.org/from-pre-k-to-college-to-global-citizenship-vincent-izuegbus-vision-for-wells-elementary/

Through monthly learning labs and leadership coaching sessions from our partners at The Center for Urban Education Leadership at University of Illinois Chicago and Wise Leadership Consulting, our fellows have made significant strides toward improving their leadership abilities and the educational outcomes in CPS.

As we reflect on our previous sessions, fellows have:
• Created goals aligned with their Leadership Development Plan.
• Participated in professional development opportunities.
• Engaged in Professional Learning Communities such as instructional leadership, organizing and analyzing systems, vision and expectations, and social-emotional learning.

Tea Time," a program that will provide opportunities for parents to learn about the school community at Bass. #CPSrunsonAPs https://t.co/ll4a6vUgaN

Assistant Principal (AP) Brandi Barrett, of Bass Elementary in Englewood, has worked in education for 26 years. Her mother was an assistant principal, providing her with a role model, so AP Barrett also wants to show her students a strong leader in whom they can see themselves. 

Throughout her tenure, AP Barrett has worked to transform parent engagement with monthly initiatives and community partnerships. Currently, she plans to launch "What's the Tea? Tea Time,” a program that will provide opportunities for parents and caregivers to learn about and contribute to the school community at Bass. “So many parents feel unwelcome in schools,” she says. “I bring in programs to create a sense of belonging and show them all things are possible.” 

She has also partnered with organizations like Team Englewood and the YMCA. These collaborations have expanded parental involvement and led to tutoring programs that empower parents to be active participants in their children’s education while supporting student well-being. 

Brandi Barrett's dedication to Bass Elementary exemplifies how APs:
• Strengthen school-community connections.
• Develop effective parent engagement strategies.
• Leverage partnerships to enrich educational experiences.
• Promote skills like digital literacy and math among parents to support student learning.

With Assistant Principal (AP) Appreciation Week just around the corner, we're excited to kick things off with AP Brandi Whitfield-Lewis at Calmeca Academy of Fine Arts and Dual Language.

Recognizing a critical challenge within Calmeca, AP Whitfield-Lewis observed that diverse-learner teachers needed help balancing competing priorities due to limited planning time. Her solution in partnership with staff was "Focus Fridays," where diverse learners join general education peers in classes to promote inclusion, anti-bullying, and social-emotional learning (SEL) while freeing up crucial planning time for teachers. 

"Focus Fridays" showcase the power of APs to: 
• Identify and address critical needs.
• Develop creative and effective solutions.
• Empower teams to collaborate and support all students.

The program's success is clear: since launching, "Focus Fridays" have significantly improved inclusion, SEL skills, and belonging for students while improving curriculum alignment and enhancing professional development for teachers across Calmeca. During the 2023-24 school year, Calmeca incorporated "Focus Friday" into its Continuous Improvement Work Plan, emphasizing its commitment to connectedness and well-being. 

Let's celebrate AP Whitfield-Lewis and all APs who make a difference! #CPSrunsonAPs

Although our approaches and geographic scope differ, IPA and The Fund are united in our effort to foster conditions that allow strong educators to lead their schools effectively. The Illinois Principal Report summarizes data about Illinois principals, offers insight into their roles and responsibilities, and highlights real leaders to reinforce the urgent need for greater decision-making autonomy.

As Latino/a/x Heritage Month comes to an end, we are excited to share the launch of a new Affinity Group Program in partnership with the Latino/a/x Leadership Pipeline (LLP) and Center Forward. Together, we aim to advance 20 aspiring leaders — 10 Latino/a/x and 10 Black — into principal and assistant principal roles within Chicago Public Schools (CPS) by 2025. 

Currently, 81.9% of CPS students identify as Latino/a/x or Black, but only 62.7% of principals identify as such. These affinity groups will help build a more diverse pipeline of school leaders that better reflects the students and communities they serve. Read more here:
